title: Thailand Floods Wreck the Hard Drive Industry: The Biggest Falls, the Second Takes the Crown
dek: A Thai flood reshuffled the hard drive hierarchy: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter-on-quarter, Seagate only 8%, and Seagate took the top spot.
why: This flood provides a complete case study of the risks of geographically concentrated manufacturing supply chains—industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single-point bottlenecks all detonate at once.
who: Production decision-makers preparing for or already operating in Southeast Asia, investors tracking the hard drive and storage industry landscape, and engineers managing supply chain risk.
skip: The opening on Thai rivers and dam-building history can be skipped; start at 3 minutes in, where the hard drive industry's move to Thailand is explained.

points.h: Flood dikes gave hard drive factories a false sense of security
points.body: The industrial estates sit on a floodplain north of Bangkok, reclaimed from rice paddies. To guard against floods, developers built ring dikes up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps, and drainage systems; the estates quickly grew into small cities with housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season hit in 2011, seven industrial estates were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this kind of seemingly complete infrastructure that created a false confidence—the belief that even if it rained, all would be well. In other words, what manufacturers bought was not safety but an illusion of risk.

points.h: Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
points.body: After the disaster, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focusing on favoritism toward farmers and rice corruption allegations. But research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios of release strategies for two dams and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could be reduced by at most 3.68%. A 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water fell directly on the disaster zone; reservoir decisions cannot bear the blame.

points.h: Why Seagate, untouched by floods, also halted
points.body: Seagate's factory in Korat was largely unaffected, but production still stopped—because seven of its top ten suppliers were flooded. A typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives; two of its plants were flooded and halted production. The hard drive supply chain is tightly interlocked: no matter how safe the final assembly line, if motors don't arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate quickly qualified new suppliers, modified designs to reduce complexity, and negotiated payment terms with suppliers, keeping its quarterly shipment decline to 8%. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant was flooded to a depth of 1.8 meters, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference was not in the height of their buildings but in which supply chain could reroute around the break faster.

points.h: Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
points.body: Before the flood, the hard drive industry had just undergone consolidation: Western Digital announced the acquisition of Hitachi's hard drive business in March 2011, and a month later Seagate announced the acquisition of Samsung, bringing supply and demand back into rough balance. Because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the impact was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that demand in Q4 2011 was about 180 million units, but actual production was only 110 to 120 million; and the flood hit right before the Christmas shopping season. Retail prices immediately rose 20% to 40%; a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected due to the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, amplified by zero inventory, became a global shortage.

points.h: Floodwaters receded, but hard drive prices stayed high for two years
points.body: The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability returned to pre-flood levels only about nine months later; retail prices fell even more slowly—prices on Newegg did not return to pre-flood levels until April 2013. Backblaze, using its own purchasing records, calculated that the cost per GB in September 2011 was $0.044, and it did not return to that level until September 2013. Why is it easier to raise prices than to lower them? The author offers several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the 2011 acquisitions by the two giants added extra costs, tablets caused a permanent decline in PC hard drive demand, and a more cynical guess—after Seagate and Western Digital acquired second-tier rivals, only three major players remained, making prices easier to 'stabilize,' or, in his words, to cartelize. He does not conclude which is the truth.

points.h: The flooded giant chose to stay and build more walls
points.body: Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not evacuate but doubled down on defense. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owners built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reason is not hard to understand: existing estates, supporting infrastructure, and skilled workers are not easy to pack up and move. Thailand has since faced more major floods, especially in the 2020s, with almost annual occurrences; in November of the most recent year, it even rained what was called a 'once-in-300-years' event, but these estates have held so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next big flood.
